subtype: Approach: guarding own time and limits [Thinking]
passage: Sunday night. A third person asked me to mentor them this week, and I said no. It was awkward. Last spring I had four mentees plus the release crunch, and I cancelled on two of them; one went quiet and I'm not sure I ever fixed that. So the rule now: two at a time, Tuesday and Thursday evenings, forty-five minutes, and I say so upfront. Hemant is one of my two, and I'd rather give Hemant a reliable slot than a maybe. Wrote to the third person offering to recommend a colleague and a date when I might have space. Felt guilty for an hour, then fine. Sessions kept beat sessions promised. — Tejas

qa.q: How many mentees does Tejas take at a time?
qa.a: Tejas takes two mentees at a time.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel after saying no to the third request?
qa.a: Tejas felt guilty for an hour and then fine, having protected the sessions already promised.

qa.q: What other approach could Tejas use for people who ask but cannot fit in?
qa.a: Tejas could run a group session once a month for those people, which shares some help without a weekly promise.

qa.q: How might Hemant see the arrangement?
qa.a: Hemant probably feels secure that sessions will happen, having a reliable slot instead of a maybe.

grounding: Shows a mentor limiting the number of mentees, stating availability clearly and keeping the commitment reliable.
